opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's trickier than it first appears. When people talk about diversity in generated faces, they often mean two different things. One is *distributional* diversity: if I generate a thousand faces, do they cover the space of human appearance reasonably well, across age, skin tone, facial structure, expression, and so on? The other is *sample-level* diversity: for a given prompt or identity, am I getting meaningfully different outputs, or is the model collapsing to a handful of modes?

For the first kind, a common starting point is to embed the generated images with a strong face representation model and look at the statistics of those embeddings. You can compare them against a reference distribution of real faces using metrics in the spirit of FID, or better, precision and recall style metrics. Those separate fidelity, meaning whether the samples look like real faces, from coverage, meaning whether they span the real distribution. A single number like FID tends to blur those together, and a model can score well while still missing whole regions of the face space.

The catch is that the embedding itself carries assumptions. Face recognition networks are trained to be invariant to things like expression, pose, and lighting, because they care about identity. So if you measure diversity in that space, you can underestimate variation that matters perceptually. We usually use several feature spaces: identity embeddings, attribute predictors for age, expression, and head pose, and more general vision-language features. Then we look at diversity along each axis rather than collapsing everything into one score.

For sample-level diversity, pairwise distances work well. You generate many samples under the same condition and measure the average dissimilarity, or you look at how many distinct identities the samples cluster into. If you ask for "a person smiling" and get twenty near-identical faces, that's a clear sign of mode collapse, even if each image looks great.

Then there's the fairness dimension, which you have to handle carefully. Attribute classifiers for perceived demographic characteristics are themselves biased and imprecise, so treating their outputs as ground truth can mislead you. I prefer to treat them as rough indicators, check them against human evaluation where possible, and report uncertainty rather than one clean percentage. Human studies are expensive, but they catch things automated metrics miss, like subtle sameness in facial features that classifiers don't flag.

So the short answer is that there's no single diversity metric. You need a combination: distribution-level coverage against real data, per-attribute breakdowns, intra-prompt variability, and some human validation. Each one alone can be gamed or misread, but together they give you a much more honest picture of what the model is actually producing.

r001.rationale: The response mentions pairwise distances between generated samples under the same condition, but does not describe comparing embeddings of multiple faces within a single generated image.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we spent a lot of time on, because the honest answer is that most of the field was measuring diversity in a way that wasn't really capturing what we cared about. The standard approach is you generate a bunch of faces, you run them through an off-the-shelf attribute classifier, and you count how many fall into each bucket for skin tone, gender, age, and so on. And that's a fine starting point, but it has a couple of problems.

The first is that you're inheriting all the biases of the classifier itself. If your skin tone classifier was trained on a dataset that's skewed, then your diversity measurement is skewed in the same direction, and you don't even know it. So one thing we do is we try to anchor to more objective, lower-level signals where we can. For skin tone, for example, we look at things like the Monk scale or perceptual lightness in a controlled color space, rather than just trusting a learned classifier to tell us "this is category three." It's not perfect, lighting and rendering style still affect it, but it's much more inspectable.

The second problem is that attribute counting treats diversity as a set of independent marginals. You might have a model that produces a nice balanced distribution across skin tones and a nice balanced distribution across age, but every older face is light-skinned and every darker face is young. So we look at the joint distribution, not just the marginals, and we specifically look at the intersections where models tend to collapse.

And then the third piece, which I think is actually the most important, is that categorical attributes miss a lot of what makes faces different from one another. Two faces can share every label you've defined and still look like the same person. So we also measure diversity in an embedding space, using face recognition features, and we look at the pairwise distances across the generated set. If those distances are collapsing, the model is essentially producing a few templates with cosmetic variation. We compare that spread against the spread you'd see in a reference set of real faces, so you have a sense of what "natural" diversity looks like rather than just picking an arbitrary threshold.

The last thing I'd say is that we always condition this on the prompt. Diversity when you ask for "a person" is a very different question from diversity when you ask for "a nurse" or "a CEO." A lot of the interesting failures only show up in those occupational or contextual prompts, so we evaluate across a structured prompt set rather than reporting one global number. One number hides too much.

r001.rationale: The response describes pairwise distances between face embeddings across a generated set, but does not say it measures diversity among faces within a single generated image.

astra-6.text:
I would start by asking what we mean by diversity. Are we talking about different identities, different facial expressions, or variation in attributes such as age and skin tone? Those are different dimensions, and a single score can hide a lot.

One approach is to represent the generated faces in a feature space and examine how broadly they’re distributed. Are we generating many distinct faces, or small variations of the same face? Then we can examine coverage across attributes and combinations of attributes. But we have to be careful, because the models used to extract those features or estimate those attributes can themselves be biased.

And diversity has to be considered alongside image quality. Distorted faces might look very different numerically, but that’s not useful diversity. So I would combine distribution-level measurements with human inspection, rather than rely on one metric.

r001.rationale: The response discusses diversity across generated faces in feature space, but does not describe measuring diversity within one image using pairwise similarities between embeddings of the faces in that image.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by asking what we mean by diversity. Are we talking about different identities, or variation in age, skin tone, facial features, expression, and pose? Those are different dimensions, and a single score can hide a lot.

One approach is to represent the faces in a feature space and look at how broadly they are distributed. Are we generating distinct identities, or slight variations of the same face? Then we can examine the distribution across attributes and combinations of attributes. You might have broad age coverage and broad skin-tone coverage separately, but still miss particular combinations.

We also have to be careful with the measurement itself. If the model extracting those features has biases, those biases carry into the diversity score. So I would combine quantitative measures with human assessment, and evaluate image quality alongside diversity. A distorted face can look very different in a feature space without representing meaningful diversity.

r001.rationale: The response discusses feature-space spread and attribute distributions generally, but does not describe measuring diversity within a single generated image using pairwise similarities between face embeddings.
